blocks.text: “The art of theater is a voyage,” wrote François Regnault, before adding: “Motionless in the middle of the city.” The line opens Navire amiral as an epigraph, set down like a compass on the chart table. It would suit the house of Molière, whose vocabulary still smells of hemp and tar: lines, pulleys, tackles, canvas. Few people know it, but in the days when sailors stayed ashore through the winter, theaters hired them to work the stage machinery. The sailors left, but their knots remained.

Stéphane Lavoué spent ten years inside this windowless hull. As associate artist at the Comédie-Française from 2015 to 2025, during Éric Ruf’s tenure, he grew steadily drawn to the trades of the shadows: stagehands, prop masters, costume makers, all those who keep the show running and never take a bow. Long days under artificial light, in the understage and the workshops. “I sometimes felt as if I were moving around inside a submarine,” he recalls. A mere image? A lead, rather. “As early as the 16th century, theater borrowed heavily from sailing ships, taking their techniques and their vocabulary,” the artist explains, and today’s stagehands “often see themselves as crew members.” Hence the journey in reverse: leaving the fly tower for the gangways, the Salle Richelieu for the Royale, as the French Navy is nicknamed.

blocks.text: Three vessels, and three closed worlds. The multi-mission frigate Bretagne , in the Iroise Sea. The nuclear ballistic missile submarine Le Téméraire , somewhere in the North Atlantic. The aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle , in the western Mediterranean. There, Stéphane Lavoué found “the same rituals, the same precision of gesture, the same need to act as one body to accomplish a shared mission.” The anaphora is a gift, so we keep it. A difficult parallel? Very. So the photographer shuffles the cards, and the book becomes a third country, its borders erased.

The captions wait at the end, gathered together, and as precise as a ship’s log. “This loss of bearings is deliberate,” Stéphane acknowledges. “It lets readers project their own stories onto the images.” Until then, everyone navigates by dead reckoning. A wig on its stand, as demure as a figurehead (Comédie-Française, 2024). Casts of actors’ faces stored in the basement of the Salle Richelieu, a gallery of plaster ancestors. A fake porthole stuck to the wall of the Bretagne ‘s cafeteria, on a 142-meter frigate with only one real porthole, in the commander’s office. An aquarium in the commanding officer’s wardroom aboard Le Téméraire , where the two crews, red and blue, share responsibility for keeping the fish alive.

blocks.text: For Stéphane Lavoué, the most powerful experience remains the submarine. “I often compare it to a trip to the Moon,” he says. “Once you’re submerged, you lose all direct connection with the outside world. You no longer know whether you’re moving forward or backward, whether it’s day or night.” Captain Nemo is not far off, library included: the one aboard Le Téméraire holds, according to the caption, the complete run of the manga The Summit of the Gods (every era has its classics). A nuclear power plant able to vanish beneath the sea for months, a crew of 110 sailors, an infirmary that turns into an operating room: a true science-fiction set.

Portraiture remains the keel of Stéphane Lavoué’s work, the man who, from Zinedine Zidane to Salman Rushdie, has photographed just about every public face France has to offer. “I didn’t just want to show professionals at work. I was trying to bring characters to the surface,” the artist says. Hence Lieutenant Julien, a Rafale fighter pilot in the ready room. Or Sébastien, known as “the Thigh,” the head chef who serves 230 meals a day in a kitchen of two square meters. Or Thomas, known as “the Sorcerer,” a nurse and radiology operator. Corsairs’ nicknames. On the theater side, Lino, César and Kevin, stagehands, and Hinda, who presses the ruffs and starched collars.

blocks.text: There remains the second captain. Éric Ruf, honorary sociétaire of the Comédie-Française and self-described “stage sailor,” contributes fragments attributed to fictional authors, drawn from fictional novels: Le Retour à Narvik (The Return to Narvik) by Knut Eleisson, Augustin le capiste (Augustin from Cap-Sizun) by Nolwenn Legars, Mon père ne m’a pas aimé (My Father Didn’t Love Me) by Sylvain Touzé (an unbeatable title). In them, a Norwegian pastor and a German captain dine in the middle of the Atlantic on April 10, 1940; a child surrounded by pirates finds, at the bottom of a chest, a single mauve satin slipper (Claudel, whose The Satin Slipper is rehearsed in the pages of the book, would approve); Jonah discovers, in the belly of the whale, that he has company. An anonymous treatise even claims that the red of Italian-style theater curtains comes from a room aboard warships, painted red so as not to frighten the wounded who were amputated there, and called “the theater.” True? False? A gangway legend. “His texts don’t explain the images; they shift them,” Stéphane Lavoué sums up. “The book works the same way,” he continues. “It deliberately sustains a degree of uncertainty and fiction.”

Born in Mulhouse in 1976, Stéphane Lavoué graduated from the École supérieure du bois, a school of wood engineering, and spent two years in the Brazilian Amazon buying timber for an industrial group before changing course in 2001. Winner of the Prix Niépce in 2018, and in 2022 one of the laureates of the major photographic commission “La France sous leurs yeux” (France Through Their Eyes), for which he photographed young army recruits, he showed Navire amiral at the Ateliers des Capucins in Brest from June 12 to September 20, 2026. The book, for its part, holds its course. And if you ask Stéphane Lavoué which image sums up the whole, he points to a corridor at the Comédie-Française, “a perspective that sinks into darkness toward an almost invisible vanishing point.” And he adds: “When I took it, I immediately thought of a submarine.”
Navire amiral by Stéphane Lavoué, with texts by Éric Ruf, is published by Atelier EXB and available for €49.
